passage: I am Reena, and last year I used to eat lunch near the popular table just in case someone waved me over. Nobody did. I felt silly all the time. One day I saw Yusuf and Meera at our own class bench, arguing about which bird was on the wall, and they looked happy. So I sat with them. I stopped watching the popular table after a few days. Now we trade stories and stickers, and I learned Meera can imitate every teacher. Being with only two friends is quiet, but I laugh more. Looking back, I did not give up on anything; I just stopped waiting.

qa.q: What were Yusuf and Meera arguing about?
qa.a: They were arguing about which bird was on the wall.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling while sitting near the popular table hoping to be waved over?
qa.a: Reena felt silly and hopeful, wanting to belong but not being noticed.

qa.q: Which change helped Reena, and why did it work?
qa.a: Reena sat with Yusuf and Meera instead of waiting, found friends who liked Reena as they were, and laughed more with them.

qa.q: How might Yusuf and Meera have seen Reena joining them?
qa.a: They probably welcomed Reena, since they went on sharing stories and stickers and included Reena easily.

grounding: A child stops chasing the popular group and enjoys their two friends; a smaller circle feels deeper.

passage: For a whole term Joseph had tried to get into the cricket gang that ruled the ground behind the church school in Kottayam. He bowled their balls back, laughed at their jokes, even carried their bats. They never picked him. One Saturday, sitting on the canal wall, he watched Madhuri and Biju racing paper boats, shouting and splashing. They waved at him every week, and every week he had waved back and walked on to the ground. Today he didn't. He climbed down, folded a boat from a notebook page and lost three races in a row. They laughed till their stomachs hurt. Walking home, Joseph realised he hadn't thought about the cricket gang all afternoon. His chest felt light.

qa.q: What did Madhuri and Biju race?
How did Joseph feel walking home?
qa.a: Light and happy, and surprised that he hadn't thought about the cricket gang all afternoon.

qa.q: What did Joseph gain by letting go of the cricket gang?
qa.a: Time and energy for Madhuri and Biju, who had waved at him every week and genuinely enjoyed his company.

qa.q: How might Madhuri and Biju see Joseph finally joining?
qa.a: Pleased; they had waved at him every week, hoping he would come.

grounding: A boy stops chasing a popular group and discovers the joy of two friends who already liked him.

passage: In Stockholm, Ingrid had spent all autumn trying to get invited to Elsa's sleepovers. She copied Elsa's braids and learned every dance video. The invitations never came. On Friday, Tomas and Aya asked her, like every Friday, to play board games at Tomas's flat. This time, instead of checking her phone for Elsa's messages, Ingrid said yes and turned it face down. They played a dragon game until they were crying with laughter, and Tomas's dad brought cinnamon buns. On the tram home, Ingrid noticed her shoulders weren't tight. She didn't feel she had lost anything. She felt she had finally arrived somewhere. She took out the braids and let her hair fall loose.

qa.q: How did Ingrid feel on the tram home, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Her shoulders weren't tight; she felt relaxed and content, as if she had finally arrived somewhere.

qa.q: Why was stopping the chase not a defeat?
qa.a: It freed Ingrid's energy for Tomas and Aya, who actually liked her and had invited her every Friday.

qa.q: How might Tomas see Ingrid turning her phone face down?
qa.a: As a sign she was really with them this time, which probably made Tomas glad 🙂

grounding: A girl in Sweden stops chasing a popular girl's approval and enjoys the friends who already like her.
